Features distinguishing late hematoma from BIA-ALCL included acute pain, absence of persistent effusion beyond 1 year, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) signal characteristics consistent with evolving blood products. Proposed mechanisms included capsular microfractures, chronic inflammation with neovascularization, external trauma, and iatrogenic factors such as anticoagulation. Ultrasound was the preferred initial screening tool; MRI provided definitive assessment of hematoma staging and implant integrity. Image-guided aspiration was essential to obtain fluid for cytology, microbiology, and CD30 immunohistochemistry to exclude BIA-ALCL. Surgical evacuation with capsulectomy was the most frequently reported definitive treatment; ultrasound-guided aspiration or arterial embolization were described in select patients with intact implants or poor surgical tolerance. Follow-up and recurrence data were inconsistently reported.

Conclusions

Late hematoma should be considered in implant recipients with delayed swelling or periprosthetic fluid. Clinical evaluation, ultrasound, MRI, and image-guided aspiration guide management. Surgical evacuation with capsulectomy remains the primary reported treatment. These findings are descriptive only.

title: Habitat-based ultrasound radiomics for preoperative prediction of axillary lymph node metastasis in breast cancer: a two-center study.
abstract: Background Accurate preoperative prediction of axillary lymph node metastasis (ALNM) remains challenging. This study investigates whether habitat-based ultrasound radiomics of suspicious axillary lymph nodes can predict preoperative ALNM in patients with breast cancer. Methods This retrospective two-center study included 416 breast cancer patients with suspicious axillary lymph nodes and pathologically confirmed nodal status. Patients from the Second Affiliated Hospital of Anhui Medical University were randomly assigned to the training and internal validation cohorts at a ratio of 7:3, whereas patients from Taihe County People's Hospital constituted the external test cohort. Suspicious lymph nodes were manually segmented. Pixel-level features were clustered using the K-means algorithm to divide each node into four habitat subregions. Radiomics features were extracted from the intranodal region of interest and each habitat subregion to construct the intranodal radiomics, individual habitat, and habitat radiomics models. A combined nomogram integrating the optimal radiomics signature with independent clinical predictors was developed. Results Cortical thickness and lymph node vascular pattern were independent predictors of ALNM. The habitat radiomics model outperformed the intranodal radiomics and individual habitat models, with areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) of 0.859, 0.809, and 0.791 in the training, internal validation, and external test cohorts, respectively. The combined nomogram achieved the highest AUCs of 0.866, 0.819, and 0.806 in the corresponding cohorts, and its clinical utility was confirmed by decision curve analysis. Conclusions Habitat-based ultrasound radiomics improved ALNM prediction by capturing intranodal heterogeneity. The nomogram may provide a practical noninvasive tool for individualized preoperative assessment of suspicious axillary lymph nodes.

title: Liposomal bupivacaine versus ropivacaine thoracic paravertebral block for thoracoscopic atrial septal defect repair: analgesic efficacy and cardiac biomarker outcomes in a single-center, assessor-blinded, randomized trial.
abstract: Background Thoracoscopic atrial septal defect (ASD) repair, although minimally invasive, can cause substantial postoperative pain. Thoracic paravertebral block (TPVB) provides effective chest wall analgesia, and liposomal bupivacaine (LB), a long-acting local anesthetic with sustained release, may prolong analgesic duration. We investigated whether ultrasound-guided TPVB using long-acting LB improves postoperative analgesia without compromising cardiovascular safety compared with ropivacaine (RP). Methods This randomized, assessor-blinded trial enrolled 94 patients undergoing thoracoscopic ASD repair, who were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive ultrasound-guided TPVB with either LB or RP. Eligibility criteria included age 18-55 years, American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) II-III, New York Heart Association (NYHA) II-III, and ejection fraction (EF) >50%. Randomization was computer-generated with sealed envelopes. Safety monitoring included continuous electrocardiography (ECG) for arrhythmias, with Clavien-Dindo grading and Naranjo causality assessment. The primary endpoint was the numerical rating scale (NRS, 0-10) pain score during coughing at 24 h postoperatively. Secondary outcomes included NRS scores at other time points, 72-h opioid consumption (morphine milligram equivalents, MME), time to first rescue analgesia, extended analgesia outcomes [postoperative days 4-7 (POD4-POD7)], perioperative hemodynamics, postoperative recovery, cardiac/inflammatory biomarker trajectories, and adverse events (with postoperative arrhythmias analyzed separately). Results Baseline demographic, clinical, and intraoperative variables were well-balanced between groups (all P>0.05). Compared with RP, LB was associated with lower NRS pain scores at rest and during coughing from extubation through 72 h (all P<0.05), including the primary endpoint at 24 h. LB significantly reduced 72-h opioid consumption [median interquartile range (IQR) 7.5 (0, 42) mg vs. 45 (30, 67.5) mg; P<0.001] and increased the proportion of patients requiring no rescue analgesia within 72 h (72.4% vs. 27.6%; P=0.003). Time to first rescue analgesia was numerically longer with LB (20.5 h vs. 12.0 h; P=0.10), and opioid-sparing effects persisted on POD4-POD7 (both P<0.001). Mechanical ventilation duration was shorter in the LB group [5 (3, 6) h vs. 6 (4, 7.5) h; P=0.03]. Cardiac and inflammatory biomarker trajectories did not differ between groups. Non-arrhythmic adverse events were comparable, and postoperative arrhythmia incidence within 30 days was similar between groups (13.3% vs. 15.6%). Conclusions In adults undergoing thoracoscopic ASD repair, LB-based TPVB provides superior early analgesia with sustained opioid sparing and shorter mechanical ventilation duration, without signals of increased cardiovascular risk, including postoperative arrhythmias. These findings support considering LB-TPVB as part of multimodal analgesia for thoracoscopic ASD repair, pending confirmation in larger multicenter studies. Trial registration ChiCTR2500112278, retrospectively registered at the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry on November 12, 2025.

title: Development and internal validation of a clinicopathological and CT radiomics based prediction model for extracranial distant metastasis after radical resection in early-stage non-small cell lung cancer.
abstract: Background Wide use of low-dose chest CT detects more early NSCLC, though recurrence (mostly extracranial distant metastasis) still occurs. This study aimed to establish and validate computed tomography (CT) radiomics models that can be used for predicting the risk of extracranial distant metastasis (EDM) after radical resection in early-stage non-small cell lung cancer (e-NSCLC). Methods This retrospective study included 312 patients with e-NSCLC who underwent radical surgery at Shandong Cancer Hospital from 2014 to 2019. The cases were randomly divided into a training set (n=200) and a validation set (n=112). The study excluded patients who received neoadjuvant therapy, had interrupted follow-up, or died of non-tumor-related causes. The patients were followed up for an average of 30.6 months after the first postoperative CT examination. This study defined EDM as distant metastasis in other organs other than brain metastasis after surgery, and accounted for 78.6% of all metastatic cases. The region of interest (ROI) was delineated, and the radiomics features were selected by using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) logistic regression models to construct radiomics signatures. The association between the radiomics signature and the occurrence of EDM was also evaluated. A combined nomogram incorporating the selected radiomics and clinical-pathological predictors was constructed using multivariable regression. The concordance index (C-index) was used to evaluate the performance of the model. To determine the clinical effectiveness of nomogram in radiomics, the decision curve analysis (DCA) was performed. Results A total of 75 patients (24.0%) experienced metastasis, with EDM accounting for 78.6%. In the overall cohort, radiomics signature were significantly associated with the occurrence of the EDM. The discrimination performance of the radiomics nomogram is significantly better than the clinical-pathologic nomogram (P<0.001), with the C-indexes 0.818 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.780-0.856] and 0.823 (95% CI: 0.769-0.877) in the training and validation cohorts, respectively. Analysis of the calibration and decision curves indicated that the comprehensive nomogram was superior to the clinical-pathological and radiomics nomogram in predicting EDM survival. Conclusions CT radiomics features have the potential to predict postoperative EDM and may assist in preliminarily identifying patients at high metastatic risk, which could provide a reference for individualized postoperative adjuvant decision-making in e-NSCLC.

title: Two parallel systems constructed from complementary optical coherence tomography and histopathology for the assessment of murine intestinal inflammation: a dual-modality assessment.
abstract: Background Quantitative assessment of intestinal inflammation among patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) remains a clinical challenge. Conventional histopathology lacks robust quantification, and a real-time, noninvasive alternative is needed. This study aimed to establish a quantitative histopathological system for IBD and to develop a corresponding optical coherence tomography (OCT) system for real-time detection. Methods Murine models for both ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn disease (CD) were developed, and corresponding intestinal histopathological samples were obtained. Artificial intelligence-based image segmentation enabled systematic analysis of pathological images, including two-dimensional planar structures, three-dimensional volumetric morphology, texture features, and grayscale histograms, through which a comprehensive histopathological evaluation system for precise quantitative assessment of intestinal inflammation severity was established. Based on this framework, an OCT system was developed for intestinal wall structural analysis, which demonstrated high concordance with histopathological benchmarks while enabling real-time, noninvasive quantitative detection. Results Both systems effectively differentiated UC, CD, and normal tissue. Planar histopathology revealed significant differences in these models in comparison to controls. The median mucosal fold angle was markedly elevated in UC [median 63.854°, interquartile range (IQR), 37.110-91.151°] and CD (49.925°, IQR, 34.140-62.550°) mice as compared controls (7.635°, IQR, 5.975-10.873°) (both P values <0.001). Submucosal area and cell count were higher in both disease groups, while the gland count was lower (all P values <0.05). Mucosal area ratio decreased from 73.608% in controls to 66.703% in UC mice (P=0.020) and to 59.182% in CD mice (P<0.001), whereas the submucosa ratio increased from 8.127% to 10.812% (P=0.031) and 16.076% (P<0.001), respectively. Three-dimensional reconstruction confirmed increased intestinal wall volumes in both disease groups (all P values <0.05). OCT texture analysis showed decreased energy and increased entropy in the UC and CD groups as compared to the control group (P<0.05), indicating disrupted microstructure. Gray-scale analysis revealed a shift toward lower values in diseased tissues (P<0.001). Pathological texture analysis demonstrated significantly elevated contrast in CD mice (median 153.425) as compared with UC (62.160) and control (70.495) mice (P<0.001), suggesting that CD and UC each have distinct textural signatures. Conclusions This work establishes an integrated framework: a quantitative histopathological system providing novel diagnostic indices, and a complementary OCT system enabling real-time assessment. It offers a proof of concept for multimodal quantitative biomarkers in IBD, an objective tool for preclinical research, and a foundation for future OCT endoscopic applications in clinical evaluation.

title: Atrial and ventricular mechanical dysfunction and myocardial injury predict long-term outcomes in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: a retrospective cohort study.
abstract: Background Left ventricular (LV) diastolic dysfunction is a hallmark of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) and imposes chronic pressure overload on the left atrium, leading to progressive atrial remodeling and functional impairment. Conventional left atrial (LA) volumetric indices reflect comparatively advanced structural alterations and are incapable of identifying early functional deterioration. The present research sought to investigate the prognostic significance of LA and LV myocardial deformation parameters obtained from cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) in patients with HCM. Methods This single-center retrospective study included 126 HCM patients and 40 healthy volunteers who underwent comprehensive CMR examinations. LA longitudinal strain (reservoir, conduit, and booster components) was assessed using the fast long-axis method; LV global strain and torsion were derived using feature-tracking analysis. Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) was quantified to assess myocardial fibrosis. Patients with HCM were followed longitudinally for the occurrence of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs). Cox regression analyses were performed to identify independent predictors of MACEs. Results Compared with healthy volunteers, patients with HCM exhibited significantly impaired LA reservoir, conduit, and booster strain, as well as reduced LV global strain parameters (all P<0.05). Following a median observational period of 1,055 days, 41 patients (32.5%) experienced MACEs. Patients with MACEs demonstrated markedly reduced LA strain and LV torsion compared with those without events. In multivariable Cox regression analysis, LA booster strain [hazard ratio (HR): 0.854, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.799-0.914], LV torsion (HR: 0.517, 95% CI: 0.298-0.895), and serum creatine kinase myocardial band (CKMB) (HR: 1.032, 95% CI: 1.018-1.047) emerged as independent predictors of MACEs. LA booster strain yielded the optimal prognostic efficacy for predicting MACEs [area under the curve (AUC): 0.827]. Conclusions LA booster strain, LV torsion, and CKMB represent complementary markers reflecting atrial function, ventricular mechanics, and myocardial injury, respectively. Their independent associations with adverse outcomes highlight the multifactorial nature of disease progression in HCM and support a more integrative approach to risk stratification beyond single-domain assessment. Incorporating these parameters into routine CMR and clinical evaluation may facilitate earlier identification of patients at increased risk for MACEs and support individualized surveillance strategies.

title: A mathematical framework for pre-mass detection of renal tissue anomalies from computed tomography scans: exploration of a biomechanical signature based on enhancement kinetics.
abstract: Background Early detection of renal cancer remains challenging, as current imaging techniques predominantly identify tumors only after a visible mass has formed. Lesions smaller than 1 cm are particularly difficult to detect reliably using routine computed tomography (CT). This study presents a novel mathematical framework for detecting early renal tissue anomalies before visible mass formation, grounded in the hypothesis that tumorigenesis induces subtle biomechanical alterations in tissue enhancement patterns that are observable on CT imaging. Methods We introduced the Local Biomechanical Index (LBI), a voxel-wise metric quantifying local deviations in Hounsfield unit values relative to an intra-patient renal reference, and a volumetric enrichment ratio (R t/g ) measuring the spatial concentration of extreme LBI values. The single-phase framework was evaluated on a random sample of 20 cases from the KiTS19 dataset using fixed parameters: a 3-mm local radius, the 99th percentile threshold, a 10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm three-dimensional (3D) window, and an enrichment threshold of 2.0. Voxel-level recall, precision, F1-score, and R t/g were calculated against the reference tumor masks and summarized using means, standard deviations (SDs), and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results Across the 20 cases, the mean recall was 0.575 (SD, 0.231; 95% CI: 0.474-0.676), the mean precision was 0.449 (SD, 0.292; 95% CI: 0.321-0.577), and the mean F1-score was 0.431 (SD, 0.221; 95% CI: 0.334-0.528). The mean R t/g was 5.223 (SD, 5.427; 95% CI: 2.842-7.604). Recall exceeded 0.50 in 11 of 20 cases (55%), while R t/g exceeded 2.0 in 14 cases (70%), indicating that candidate anomalies were frequently concentrated within tumor-associated regions. Because KiTS19 provides tumor annotations but does not annotate all other renal abnormalities, the reported precision represents agreement with the reference tumor masks rather than definitive precision for detecting all renal anomalies. Conclusions These findings provide preliminary evidence that early tumor-related biomechanical alterations may be detectable through spatial analysis of enhancement deviations in CT images. The proposed framework operates without tumor segmentation, relies on interpretable statistical measures, and can be fully automated. Although further validation on large longitudinal datasets is required, this approach opens a promising research direction for segmentation-free early detection of renal cancer and for integrating biomechanical signatures into radiological screening workflows.

title: Deep learning-based segmentation, grading and genotype classification of glioma: a literature analysis.
abstract: Background and objective Glioma represents the most prevalent and lethal primary brain tumor in adults, and its high mortality poses a significant challenge to clinical decision-making. While the conventional gold standard for diagnosis relies on the examination of surgically resected tumor tissue, recent advances in artificial intelligence, particularly deep learning, have demonstrated compelling performance in medical image analysis, offering the potential for non-invasive prediction of the genetic and histological features of glioma as well as automatic tumor segmentation. This review aims to comprehensively summarize deep learning-based techniques for glioma segmentation, grading, and genotype classification. Methods A systematic literature search was conducted across PubMed, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) Xplore, and Scopus for articles published in English between January 2014 and December 2025, using combinations of the terms "glioma", "brain tumor", "deep learning", "convolutional neural network", "segmentation", "classification", "grading", "genotype", "isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)", "1p/19q", and "O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT)". Peer-reviewed studies that applied deep learning methods to glioma analysis using medical imaging data and reported quantitative performance results were included, whereas review articles without original results, studies using exclusively non-deep-learning methods, and studies focused solely on non-glioma brain tumors were excluded. Key content and findings This review first summarizes the commonly used public datasets [Brain Tumor Segmentation (BraTS), The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA), The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), synthetic, and private cohorts] and performance metrics, and then surveys deep learning-based approaches for glioma segmentation, grading, and genotype classification according to task. Recent methodological advances, including Vision Transformers, foundation models such as the segment anything model (SAM) and MedSAM, diffusion models, and self-supervised learning, are also discussed. Reported performance varies considerably across datasets and evaluation protocols, and risks of bias, including slice-level data leakage, patient overlap across public repositories, and single-center confounding, remain prevalent in the genotype prediction literature. Conclusions Deep learning has become a transformative tool for non-invasive glioma characterization. Future research should prioritize prospective multi-center validation, standardized evaluation protocols, calibrated uncertainty estimation, and clinically deployable frameworks, thereby facilitating the translation of these techniques into routine diagnostic workflows and ultimately improving outcomes for patients with glioma.

title: Left ventricular function and volumes from cardiac magnetic resonance and gated [<sup>13</sup>N]-ammonia positron emission tomography myocardial perfusion imaging in patients with ischemia with no obstructive coronary arteries: a prospective head-to-head comparison using hybrid positron emission tomography/magnetic resonance.
abstract: Background Electrocardiogram (ECG)-gated 13 N-ammonia positron emission tomography (PET) myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI) has been widely validated for the assessment of left ventricular (LV) volumes and function. This study aimed to compare the accuracy of LV volumes and functional parameters derived from 13 N-ammonia PET with those obtained by cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), using CMR as the reference standard. Methods A total of 75 consecutive patients with known or suspected ischemia with no obstructive coronary arteries (INOCA) who simultaneously underwent ECG-gated 13 N-ammonia PET and CMR using a hybrid PET/magnetic resonance (MR) scanner were enrolled in this prospective study. Left ventricular end-diastolic volume (LVEDV), left ventricular end-systolic volume (LVESV), left ventricular stroke volume (LVSV), left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), and regional wall motion score (RWMS) were derived from both imaging modalities and compared using correlation and Bland-Altman (BA) analyses. Additionally, inter- and intraobserver variability in LV volumetric parameters and LVEF were evaluated for both imaging modalities. Results The correlation between PET and CMR was strong for LV volumes (r>0.83) and moderate for LVEF (r=0.65). The moderate LVEF correlation may be partially explained by the narrow range of LVEF values across the study cohort. Moreover, the agreement between 13 N-ammonia PET and CMR for LVEF was good, with minimal bias (-0.57%); however, 13 N-ammonia PET systematically underestimated LV volumes, with negative biases for LVEDV (-7.76 mL), LVESV (-3.28 mL), and LVSV (-5.33 mL). Similar, strong correlations and good agreement were observed in patients with reduced myocardial flow reserve (MFR). For both PET and CMR, inter- and intraobserver agreement for LV volumes and LVEF was high and comparable between the two modalities. In addition, RWMSs derived from ECG-gated 13 N-ammonia PET and CMR also exhibited good agreement (kappa =0.84±0.02). Conclusions LVEF and RWMS can be reliably and accurately quantified by ECG-gated 13 N-ammonia PET, although LV volumes are systematically underestimated compared with those quantified by CMR. ECG-gated 13 N-ammonia PET may serve as a complementary modality for the assessment of LV systolic function; however, CMR remains the benchmark for LV volumetric measurement and myocardial tissue assessment.

title: TiLCA-Net: nuclei segmentation and classification in pathological images via task-specialized attention and efficient decoding.
abstract: Background Nuclei segmentation and classification in whole-slide images (WSIs) are critical for tumor diagnosis and treatment. Existing methods often face multi-task feature conflict and computational redundancy. This study aimed to develop an efficient multi-task framework that balances segmentation accuracy and inference efficiency. Methods To seek an improved balance between segmentation accuracy and efficiency, this study proposes TiLCA-Net, a network that integrates multi-scale attention mechanisms with a lightweight decoding strategy to optimize comprehensive model performance. First, a Task-Specialized Attention Integrated Encoder (TSEncoder) is designed to decouple features by assigning spatial, global, and channel attention at multiple levels, thereby mitigating negative transfer. Second, we introduce an iterative cross-enhancement (ICE) module, which utilizes closed-loop iteration and median pooling to enhance global geometric consistency and robustness. Finally, a Lightweight Context Aggregation Decoder (LCA-Decoder) is introduced, replacing redundant structures with multi-scale aggregation to substantially reduce computational cost while preserving high-frequency details. Results Experiments on CoNSeP, MoNuSeg, and CervCell-Seg demonstrate that TiLCA-Net achieves a favorable balance between segmentation performance and computational efficiency. TiLCA-Net achieved mean panoptic quality (PQ) scores of 0.528, 0.578, and 0.592 on CoNSeP, MoNuSeg, and CervCell-Seg, respectively, compared with 0.504, 0.563, and 0.578 for HoVer-Net. These results indicate PQ improvements of 0.024, 0.015, and 0.014 on the three datasets, respectively. Patch-level benchmarking showed that TiLCA-Net required fewer floating point operations per second (FLOPs) and achieved higher batch throughput than HoVer-Net, but with higher single-patch latency and peak graphics processing unit (GPU) memory. Conclusions Through feature decoupling and efficient decoder reconstruction, TiLCA-Net provides a practical accuracy-efficiency trade-off for patch-level nuclei analysis in computational pathology.

title: Prediction of late-pregnancy pelvic floor dysfunction: a nomogram model based on proton density fat fraction and synthetic magnetic resonance imaging.
abstract: Background Pelvic floor dysfunction (PFD) is a highly prevalent condition that significantly compromises women's quality of life. To date, the majority of studies and clinical rehabilitation interventions have focused on the assessment and management of pelvic floor muscle (PFM) function in the postpartum period, whereas investigations into the monitoring of pelvic floor function during the third trimester of pregnancy remain relatively understudied. This study aimed to develop a radiology-clinical nomogram integrating proton density fat fraction (PDFF; Iterative Decomposition of water and fat with Echo Asymmetry and Least-squares estimation, IDEAL-IQ sequence), synthetic magnetic resonance imaging (MAGnetic Resonance Image Compilation, MAGiC sequence), and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) for predicting PFD in late pregnancy. Methods A total of 114 third-trimester pregnant women were classified into PFD and non-PFD groups. Fat fraction (FF), T1, T2, proton density (PD), and fractional anisotropy (FA) of bilateral levator ani muscles (LAMs) were measured from IDEAL-IQ, MAGiC, and DTI by two radiologists (with 15 years of experience). Measurement reliability was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). Univariate analysis screened potential predictors [age, gestational week, gravida, parity, delivery mode, fetal weight, pre- and post-pregnancy body mass index (BMI), and quantitative imaging parameters]. Significant variables were included in a multivariate logistic regression to build the nomogram. Model performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, calibration plots, and decision curve analysis (DCA). Results Of 114 participants, 52 were assigned to the PFD group and 62 to the non-PFD group. Univariate analysis showed significant between-group differences in gestational week (P=0.025), gravida (P=0.032), parity (P=0.023), fetal weight (P<0.001), left LAM FF (L-LAM FF, P=0.005), and right LAM T2 (R-LAM T2, P=0.004). The final Akaike information criterion (AIC)-selected multivariable prediction model, gravida, L-LAM FF, and R-LAM T2 were retained as nomogram predictors. The nomogram achieved moderate discrimination with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.726 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.632-0.815]. Calibration indicated good model fit, and DCA demonstrated positive net benefit within a threshold probability range of 25-83%. Interobserver agreement was moderate/excellent (ICC 0.49-0.86). FA was only an exploratory imaging biomarker and was not retained in the final combined prediction model. Conclusions The nomogram incorporating gravida, L-LAM FF, and R-LAM T2 effectively predicts PFD in late pregnancy.

title: Fully automatic airway segmentation in CT images via dual-stage neural network with topology-constrained centerline completion.
abstract: Background Precise segmentation of airways from computed tomography (CT) images is critical for pre-procedural planning in navigational bronchoscopy; however, existing methods often suffer from distal branch fractures and morphological losses due to slender diameters, low contrast, and noise. To address these limitations and achieve accurate, topologically complete airway segmentation, this study proposed a novel dual-stage neural network with topology-constrained centerline completion. Methods A two-stage centerline-guided network (TSC-Net) was developed that innovatively combines centerline structural similarity (CSS) loss and centerline overlap rate (COR) loss. CSS loss maintains the continuity of airway tree structures by strengthening centerline morphological constraints, while COR loss enhances global centerline overlap to ensure branch integrity. Additionally, a topology-difference-driven fracture-region completion mechanism was adopted to adaptively repair the fracturedand misclassified areas. The model employs a residual UNet (ResUNet) backbone integrated with an atrous spatial pyramid pooling (ASPP) module to capture multi-scale contextual features and adopts a two-stage training strategy in which the encoder is frozen during stage 2 while the decoder is fine-tuned using dynamically adjusted loss weights. This strategy enables targeted optimization of discontinuous regions without compromising globally well-predicted areas. Results Experiments on the Airway Tree Modeling Challenge 2022 (ATM'22), Lung Image Database Consortium and Image Database Resource Initiative (LIDC-IDRI), Extraction of Airways from CT (EXACT'09), and private datasets showed that TSC-Net achieved a Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 93.2%±2.1%, significantly outperforming SwinUNETR (92.9%±3.6%, P<0.05), nnUNet (91.2%±1.2%, P<0.05), and UNet (75.6%±4.3%, P<0.05). The tree-length detection (TD) rate reached 95.5%±4.2%, and the branch detection (BD) rate reached 92.6%±3.6%, both of which were significantly higher than those of all baseline methods (P<0.01). Moreover, the segmented distal branches exhibited continuous and smooth morphology. Conclusions Overall, our method significantly enhanced both segmentation accuracy and distal branch integrity in automated CT-based airway segmentation through multi-dimensional feature enhancement, topological constraint optimization, and a dynamic completion mechanism. This method holds great promise for pre-procedural planning in robotic-assisted bronchoscopy by enabling accurate visualization of peripheral airways and facilitating navigation to distant pulmonary targets.

title: Structural alterations in the superior temporal gyrus associated with depressive symptoms in migraine without aura: a voxel-based morphometry and surface-based morphometry magnetic resonance imaging study.
abstract: Background Migraine without aura (MwoA) frequently co-occurs with depressive symptoms, yet the neurobiological mechanisms underlying this comorbidity remain insufficiently characterized. This study integrated voxel-based morphometry (VBM) and surface-based morphometry (SBM) to compare gray matter volume (GMV) and cortical morphology between patients with MwoA and healthy controls (HC) and to further determine whether structural brain alterations vary across MwoA subgroups stratified by depressive symptom severity, thereby identifying potential structural correlates of depressive symptoms in this population. Methods A total of 67 patients with MwoA {38 with lower depressive symptoms [MwoA-LS, 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD-17) <8] and 29 with higher depressive symptoms (MwoA-HS, HAMD-17 ≥8)} and 40 HC were included. High-resolution T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data were processed using CAT12 to derive GMV, cortical thickness (CT), local gyrification index (LGI), sulcal depth (SD), and fractal dimension (FD). Between-group comparisons were conducted using two-sample t-tests within a general linear model framework, with sex, education, total intracranial volume (TIV) (for VBM), mean CT (for SBM), and Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAMA) scores included as covariates. Statistical significance was defined using a voxel-/vertex-level threshold of P<0.001 (uncorrected), followed by cluster-level false discovery rate (FDR) correction at q<0.05. Results Compared with HC, patients with MwoA exhibited significant reductions in GMV in the left amygdala (cluster size =305; FDR-corrected q=0.046), left parahippocampal gyrus (cluster size =273; q=0.036), left lingual gyrus (two clusters, size =218, q=0.046 and size =177, q=0.046), and right angular gyrus extending into the middle occipital gyrus and precuneus (cluster size =427; q=0.036). No significant between-group differences were observed in any SBM measure. In the subgroup analysis, patients in the MwoA-HS group showed significantly lower LGI in the right superior temporal gyrus than those in the MwoA-LS group (cluster size =73; FDR-corrected q=0.019). Exploratory partial correlation analyses indicated that no imaging metric was significantly associated with HAMD-17 scores or other clinical measures after FDR correction (all q>0.05). Conclusions Patients withMwoA exhibited widespread GMV reductions across brain regions involved in emotional and pain-related processing. In addition, patients with higher depressive symptom levels showed a distinct cortical morphological feature characterized by lower LGI in the right superior temporal gyrus, which was not detected by VBM. Given the exploratory nature of these findings, the lack of significant brain-clinical correlations after correction for multiple comparisons, and the cross-sectional study design, these results should be validated in larger longitudinal cohorts.

title: Diagnostic Performance and Clinical Outcomes of Intraoperative Neuromonitoring in Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis: A Comprehensive Analysis of 5,206 Patients.
abstract: Background Curve-specific risk factors for intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM) alerts during surgery for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) remain unclear. Methods We identified 5,206 patients with AIS who underwent spinal fusion with multimodal IONM from a prospective database. Alerts were defined as ≥50% amplitude decrease in somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEPs) and/or transcranial motor evoked potentials (TcMEPs), or >10% SSEP latency increase. Demographics, radiographic parameters, surgical variables, triggering events, interventions, and outcomes were compared between the 252 patients with and 4,954 without an alert. Results IONM alerts occurred in 5% of patients. Alert rates varied by Lenke classification, with Type-4 curves demonstrating the highest risk (8%; relative risk [RR] = 1.61, 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.15 to 2.24) and Type 5 demonstrating the lowest risk (2%; RR = 0.45, 95% CI, 0.25 to 0.82). Patients with an alert had a larger mean preoperative major Cobb angle (66.7° ± 15.0° versus 56.1° ± 12.1°, p < 0.001) and more frequent use of Ponte osteotomies (79% versus 66%, p < 0.001). Multivariable analysis demonstrated the major Cobb angle to be the leading independent risk factor for alerts (p < 0.001). Hypotension was the leading triggering event (23%), and raising blood pressure was the most common intervention overall (52%). Neurologic deficits occurred in 4% of patients with an alert versus <1% of those without an alert (p < 0.001). Only 12 patients (<1%) experienced neurologic deficits, with 2 having permanent deficits. At 2-year follow-up, the major Cobb angle correction did not differ significantly between the groups with and without alerts, alert status did not independently affect correction (p = 0.058), and the groups achieved similar outcomes (73% versus 71% correction, respectively). Conclusions IONM alerts occurred in 5% of patients with AIS and were independently associated with a larger major Cobb angle. Fewer than 1% of patients sustained a permanent neurologic injury, and alerts did not appear to compromise 2-year correction. Level of evidence Prognostic Level III. title: Classification of Forearm Involvement in Multiple Hereditary Exostoses: Consensus from the CoULD Study Group.
abstract: Background Existing classifications for forearm deformity in multiple hereditary exostoses (MHE) have demonstrated low interrater reliability and limited clinical applicability. Our primary research question was whether a Delphi consensus process could generate a more reliable and clinically useful classification for longitudinal surveillance of MHE-related forearm deformities. Methods Fifteen pediatric hand surgeons from the Congenital Upper Limb Difference (CoULD) Study Group participated in 7 rounds of online Delphi surveys (June 2022 to September 2023). An investigator team facilitated the process with anonymized feedback. Round 1 identified key clinical and radiographic features. Subsequent rounds refined these features, determined categorical structure, and piloted the system with representative radiographs. Consensus was defined as ≥70% agreement. After final consensus, interrater reliability was tested by 4 independent surgeons who classified 101 radiographs from 67 patients with forearm MHE. Reliability was assessed with kappa and concordance coefficients and compared with the Masada, Gottschalk, and Jo classifications. Results The Delphi process identified radiographic predictors that included ulnar variance, the radial articular angle (RAA), radial head alignment, and osteochondroma size. Consensus favored a 3-tier classification: Type 1, mild; Type 2, moderate; and Type 3, severe. Closing consensus was achieved, with 93% agreement. Reliability testing showed moderate agreement on the first reading (kappa = 0.55), significantly higher than for the Masada (kappa = 0.21 [original classification], kappa = 0.35 [modified version]), Gottschalk (kappa = 0.43), and Jo (kappa = 0.43) classifications. After refinement that incorporated osteochondroma size and the radial head subtypes (3A, subluxation, and 3B, dislocation), agreement improved to substantial (kappa = 0.64) (p < 0.001), with high concordance (0.82). Conclusions The CoULD MHE Classification, developed through expert consensus, integrates validated radiographic predictors with defined thresholds. It demonstrated significantly improved reliability over prior systems and provides a practical framework for longitudinal monitoring of forearm deformities in patients with MHE. Level of evidence Diagnostic Level V. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

Consensus favored a 3-tier classification: Type 1, mild; Type 2, moderate; and Type 3, severe. Closing consensus was achieved, with 93% agreement. Conclusions

The CoULD MHE Classification, developed through expert consensus, integrates validated radiographic predictors with defined thresholds. It demonstrated significantly improved reliability over prior systems and provides a practical framework for longitudinal monitoring of forearm deformities in patients with MHE.

title: Ability of Deep Learning to Predict Surgical Recommendations for Distal Radial Fractures: A Feasibility Study.
abstract: Background Distal radial fractures (DRFs) are extremely common, and decisions regarding operative intervention rely on clinical judgment and radiographic parameters at and after injury. Understanding whether a recommendation will be made for operative versus nonoperative management in an initial point-of-care setting can assist in patient counseling and reinforce timely follow-up with general orthopaedic or hand specialists. This study investigated the feasibility of using artificial intelligence (AI) to predict whether a fellowship-trained hand surgeon would recommend operative intervention using pre-reduction radiographs and clinical and demographic data. Methods A convolutional neural network (CNN) model was trained on pre-reduction injury radiographs, and its outputs were combined with clinical and demographic data in a random forest (RF) model. The final model was evaluated on a hold-out test data set. To enhance interpretability, gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) heatmaps and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were employed to identify image regions and clinical features contributing to model predictions. Results Of 1,040 included patients, 884 were used for training and 156 for testing model performance. On the test data set, the combined model achieved an accuracy of 87.14%, sensitivity of 97%, specificity of 73%, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.96, and Brier score of 0.10. Grad-CAM visualizations indicated that the CNN focused on clinically relevant features, such as fracture displacement, and SHAP analysis of the RF model highlighted age and lateral wrist radiographs as key contributors to predictions. Conclusions This pilot study demonstrates the feasibility of using AI to predict the recommendations of a group of fellowship-trained hand surgeons at 1 institution regarding operative versus nonoperative treatment for a DRF on the basis of pre-reduction injury radiographs and clinical and demographic data. Future work will focus on external validation, expanding data sets, and incorporating additional imaging features to optimize performance and generalizability. Level of evidence Prognostic Level III . See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

title: Validation of the Bone-RADS (Bone Reporting and Data System) Score for Predicting Risk of Malignancy.
abstract: Background Bone-RADS (Bone Reporting and Data System) is a consensus guideline by the American College of Radiology to assist in the risk stratification of lytic bone lesions. A score is calculated using 5 radiographic factors and a history of primary malignancy. The purpose of this study was to externally validate the Bone-RADS scoring system. Methods This retrospective review examined radiographs from January 1, 2021, to December 31, 2021. Radiographs were identified via a keyword search for "lucent," "osteolytic," or "lytic" in extremity radiograph reports. All radiographs were initially read by a musculoskeletal radiologist. Radiographs of skeletally immature patients, lesions in a bone other than a long bone, primary soft-tissue masses, and negative/normal radiographs were excluded. Radiographs were independently scored on the basis of the Bone-RADS system by 4 reviewers. In the absence of a biopsy, a lesion was considered benign if it remained stable for 2 years on radiographs. Scores were correlated with final diagnoses to calculate the rates of malignancy and malignant transformation. Results Of 1,108 screened radiographs, 423 were eligible. The mean age of the patients was 62 years and 49% were male. A higher Bone-RADS score was associated with a malignant diagnosis (p < 0.001), with an odds ratio of 9.7 (95% confidence interval [CI], 6.2 to 14.9) per 1-unit increase in the score. A higher margin score (p < 0.001), endosteal erosion (p < 0.001), a pathologic fracture (p < 0.001), and a soft-tissue mass (p = 0.02) were associated with increased risk of malignancy. The mean inter-rater agreement (weighted kappa) was 0.52, the inter-rater mean absolute deviation (MAD) was 0.37, and the intra-rater MAD was 0.27. Sensitivity was 97.1% (CI, 94.4% to 98.5%), specificity was 67.4% (CI, 59.3% to 74.5%), positive predictive value was 85.2% (CI, 80.9% to 88.7%), and negative predictive value was 92.4% (CI, 85.7% to 96.1%). Conclusions The Bone-RADS scoring system demonstrated moderate diagnostic performance for malignancy risk stratification of lytic bone lesions, with high sensitivity and reproducible binary classification of possibly benign versus malignant. Although inter-rater agreement for the 4-tier score was only moderate, clinically relevant benign-versus-malignant categorization demonstrated higher inter- and intra-rater agreement. These findings support Bone-RADS as a practical triage framework based on musculoskeletal imaging of lytic bone lesions. Level of evidence Diagnostic Level III. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

title: Extra-Articular Malunions and Nonunions of the Scapular Body and Neck: A Comparison of Functional Outcomes Before and After Reconstruction.
abstract: Background Malunions and nonunions of scapular neck and body fractures can cause considerable pain and disability. This study reports outcomes regarding functional measures, range of motion, and strength before and after reconstruction. Methods This retrospective case series at a Level-1 trauma center between 2003 and 2024 identified 50 consecutive patients (mean age, 50.3 years; 82% male; 80% White) with symptomatic malunion or nonunion of a scapular neck and/or body fracture who were referred to a single surgeon. Medial-lateral displacement and angular deformity were corrected through surgical reconstruction and malunion osteotomy. The Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand (DASH) score, range of motion, strength, and postoperative procedures requiring a return to the operating room were recorded. Results Fifty patients were included in the study; 5 patients were lost to follow-up before 12 months, leaving 45 patients (40 with malunion and 5 with nonunion) with >1-year outcomes. Eleven patients underwent reconstruction between 6 weeks and 3 months after injury because of the severity of the injury, their symptoms, and/or the necessity of an osteotomy. The median time from injury to reconstruction was 10 months (interquartile range [IQR] width, 16 months), and the median follow-up was 28.9 months (IQR width, 23.2 months). All patients achieved radiographic evidence of union. No intraoperative complications occurred. There was a mean 30.7-point improvement between the preoperative and final postoperative DASH scores (p < 0.001). The mean postoperative DASH score was 14.1 in patients who underwent reconstruction between 6 weeks and 3 months and was 23.2 in those who underwent reconstruction after 3 months. Forward flexion and abduction demonstrated significant increases in both range of motion and strength from preoperatively to postoperatively. External rotation range of motion and strength showed no significant increases. Subsequent procedures were performed in 12 patients: 8 patients underwent symptomatic implant removal (1 also underwent concurrent manipulation under anesthesia), 1 patient underwent open reduction and internal fixation for a new fracture, 2 patients underwent implant revision (1 also underwent concurrent manipulation under anesthesia), and 1 patient underwent manipulation under anesthesia for shoulder contracture. Conclusions Extra-articular scapular malunions and nonunions can be associated with considerable pain and disability. Deformity correction improved range of motion and strength and reduced disability in this cohort. A principled reconstruction can be successful in addressing the sequelae of displaced scapular fractures. Level of evidence Therapeutic Level IV. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

title: Intraoperative recognition of low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm masquerading as a right ovarian tumor: a case report
abstract: Abstract Background Low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm (LAMN) is a mucin-producing epithelial tumor arising from the appendix. When the appendix is displaced into the pelvis and becomes cystically enlarged, LAMN may mimic a right ovarian mucinous tumor. Because rupture of LAMN may cause mucin spillage and pseudomyxoma peritonei, accurate intraoperative recognition and careful surgical handling are important. Case presentation: A 75-year-old Japanese woman was referred to our department with a right adnexal mass suspected to be an ovarian tumor. Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging revealed an approximately 7-cm cystic mass in the right adnexal region, and a right ovarian mucinous tumor was suspected preoperatively. Serum carcinoembryonic antigen was mildly elevated, whereas carbohydrate antigen 19 − 9 and cancer antigen 125 were not markedly elevated. Laparoscopic surgery was performed under the preoperative diagnosis of a right ovarian tumor. Intraoperatively, the uterus and bilateral adnexa were grossly normal. Instead, a cystic mass was identified near the right adnexal region and was continuous with the appendix and ileocecal region. The lesion was carefully resected without intraoperative rupture or mucin spillage. Intraoperative frozen section analysis showed no evidence of malignancy, and ascites cytology was negative. Histopathological examination revealed LAMN with a negative surgical margin. Immunohistochemical findings were consistent with an appendiceal origin and supported the diagnosis of LAMN. Postoperative computed tomography showed no evidence of residual disease or pseudomyxoma peritonei. Conclusion LAMN can mimic a right ovarian tumor. In right-sided mucinous adnexal masses, appendiceal origin should be considered, and rupture-free complete resection is essential to prevent pseudomyxoma peritonei.

title: Graph-Aware Medical Image Intelligence: A Comparative Study of CNNs, GNNs, and Multimodal LLMs for Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia Subtyping
abstract: Abstract The correct determination of the cell type of an acute leukaemia (ALL) is essential, since therapy depends on the morphological variations that can be seen in blood smear images. Manual microscopy is still a time-consuming, labor-intensive method and the results of the diagnosis often differ from one observer to another, which is the reason for the need of reliable automatic diagnostic models. This study compares and evaluates three deep learning paradigms - Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), and multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs) - for the classification of four ALL subtypes from the Multi Cancer Dataset (4000 images). The CNN models used were trained with the same preprocessing steps, including resizing, normalization and augmentation, to promote generalization to other tasks. Based on the spatially segmented nuclei and morphological features, four GNN models were designed to capture inter-cell relationships that are not captured by pixel-based architectures. Furthermore, a multimodal model ViT–BERT and its fine-tuned version were also used to incorporate visual embeddings and text domain knowledge. The tuned ViT–BERT model achieved F1 = 0.99, matching the top CNN baselines (DenseNet121, MobileNetV2 at F1 = 0.98) and outperforming InceptionV3 and ResNet50. The graph-based reasoning models were found to perform competitively on the subtypes with unique spatial arrangement of cells, showing the importance of reasoning on graphs. Interpretability was addressed through Grad-CAM for CNN and multimodal models, and GNN Explainer for graph architectures, being transparent in model decisions. The results suggest that the pixel-level, graph-level, and multimodal representations are effective in enhancing accuracy and interpretability, which helps to build more reliable diagnostic systems for ALL.

title: Design of the Precision Medicine for more Oxygen Interstitial Lung Disease (P4O2-ILD) study: a Dutch prospective observational cohort study to identify risk factors and biomarkers for progressive fibrotic interstitial lung diseases
abstract: Abstract Background: Pulmonary fibrosis is a common end-stage manifestation of a wide range of interstitial lung diseases (ILDs). Progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF) is currently defined by longitudinal deterioration in symptoms, lung function, and/or radiological findings, often indicating that substantial and irreversible lung damage has already occurred. Consequently, the optimal timing of therapeutic intervention remains a matter of ongoing debate, highlighting the need for earlier identification of patients at risk of developing a progressive fibrotic phenotype. The P4O2 ILD study aims to identify risk factors and biomarkers associated with the development of PPF and clinically significant ILD. Methods: The P4O2 ILD study is a prospective observational cohort study that will enroll 450 participants from hospitals across the Netherlands. Three arms of participants will be included: (1) patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis or fibrotic ILD in the context of familial pulmonary fibrosis carrying pathogenic variants in established pulmonary fibrosis-associated genes (n = 150); (2) patients with other fibrotic ILDs, including idiopathic fibrotic bronchiolocentric interstitial pneumonia, fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, idiopathic fibrotic nonspecific interstitial pneumonia, connective tissue disease-associated ILD, and unclassifiable ILD (n = 150); and (3) individuals with interstitial lung abnormalities (ILA) (n = 150). Participants will undergo serial assessments over a five-year follow-up period, comprising eight study visits. Evaluations include blood sampling for peripheral blood mononuclear cells and plasma analyses, pulmonary function testing, chest computed tomography, exposome and multi-omics profiling, patient-reported outcome measures, and lower airway sampling using the particles in exhaled air technique. A subgroup of participants will additionally undergo bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage. Discussion: To identify biomarkers associated with the onset and progression of pulmonary fibrosis, the study will compare ILD subtypes that differ in their for and the rate and timing of fibrotic progression. Findings will be interpreted in the context of data obtained from a population-based healthy cohort and a cohort at increased risk of lung disease (P4O2-PARASOL). This comprehensive approach is expected to facilitate earlier detection of disease progression, improve patient stratification, guide treatment strategies, and support prevention and monitoring efforts in individuals with ILA. Trial Registration: This prospective observational cohort study is registered on 23th of September 2024 in the International Clinical Trial Registry, www.clinicaltrials.gov; IDNCT06644144. Trial Status: Recruitment began on 28-11-2024 and is ongoing. As of 14-8-2026, 37 of the planned 450 participants have been enrolled. If recruitment targets are not reached within three years, the inclusion period will be extended until the target sample size is achieved.

title: Pleomorphic Adenoma of the Upper Lip: A Case Report with Histopathological and Clinical Correlation
abstract: Abstract Background Pleomorphic adenoma (PA), often called benign mixed tumour is the most common salivary gland neoplasm. Majority of the tumours occur in major salivary glands from while only 10% occurs in minor salivary glands. Cases of PA in the oral cavity have been mainly reported in palate and respectively in the upper lip. Case presentation In this case report, we describe a case of pleomorphic adenoma with a rare clinical feature. A 49-year-old female reported to the dental hospital with a complain of slowly developing reddish-yellow coloured painless swelling in the left upper labial vestibule since 5 years. Temporary pain and temperature sensitivity have also been reported. Radiographically, there is no evidence of any radiolucency. Hence, Lipoma, mucocele, minor salivary gland tumour was considered as the differential diagnosis as these lesions are also reported in the upper lip, and they can show these clinical features. An excisional biopsy was taken. It shows a biphasic proliferation of epithelial cells and myoepithelial cells in cords and well-defined aggregates in a mixed myxoid/chondroid stroma. It shows a well-circumscribed lesion features typical for PA of the upper lip. The post-operative period was uneventful, and on 3-month follow-up, no recurrence was noted. Conclusions Pleomorphic adenoma of the upper lip is an uncommon benign neoplasm that should be included in the differential diagnosis of persistent mucosal swellings. This case highlights the importance of histopathological confirmation to ensure optimal patient outcomes.

title: BioPretext: A Multimodal Self-Supervised Learning Framework for Orthopedic Feature Extraction via Cross-Modal Signal Alignment and Dynamic Fusion
abstract: Abstract We propose BioPretext, a multimodal self-supervised learning (SSL) framework that unifies geometric and non-geometric biological signals for orthopedic feature extraction. Unlike conventional approaches that process imaging data independently, BioPretext exploits interactions between structural and functional modalities through cross-modal pretext tasks. The framework employs a dual-branch transformer architecture, where a vision transformer encodes geometric data (e.g., radiographs) and a temporal transformer processes sequential biological signals (e.g., EKG). Both representations are projected into a shared latent space via cross-attention. To improve robustness, two contrastive pretext tasks—signal inversion and time-window masking—are introduced, enabling recovery of corrupted or missing biological signals using geometric context. Extracted features are then integrated through a gated attention mechanism that adaptively weights modality contributions according to task relevance. The framework can replace conventional feature extraction modules in orthopedic AI systems and be readily applied to downstream tasks such as joint kinematics prediction and lesion segmentation. Key innovations include cross-modal SSL optimization, temporal-spatial alignment, and patient-specific dynamic fusion. Implemented with Swin Transformer and Performer backbones, BioPretext is pretrained on unlabeled multimodal datasets and subsequently fine-tuned for orthopedic applications. Experimental results demonstrate superior performance over unimodal SSL approaches, particularly in tasks involving complex interactions between biological and structural data, such as gait analysis and osteoarthritis grading. These findings highlight the potential of BioPretext as a scalable and generalizable framework for multimodal representation learning in orthopedics.

title: Hearing impairment is associated with impaired glymphatic function in middle- and older-aged adults: evidence from DTI-ALPS imaging
abstract: Abstract Hearing impairment is a common age-related sensory disorder and has been increasingly linked to central nervous system changes beyond peripheral auditory dysfunction. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between hearing impairment and glymphatic system function using the diffusion tensor imaging along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index, and to explore its potential as an imaging biomarker in middle- and older-aged adults. A total of 131 participants aged 45–80 years were enrolled, including 71 individuals with normal hearing and 60 with hearing impairment defined by pure-tone average thresholds ≥ 25 dB HL. All participants underwent brain MRI with diffusion tensor imaging, and glymphatic function was evaluated using the DTI-ALPS index. Cognitive function was assessed using the Mini-Mental State Examination and Montreal Cognitive Assessment. Associations between pure-tone average and DTI-ALPS indices were examined using Spearman correlation analysis. Logistic regression models were applied to identify independent factors associated with hearing impairment, and receiver operating characteristic analysis was used to evaluate diagnostic performance. Participants with hearing impairment were older, more frequently male, and exhibited lower MoCA scores compared with controls. Global and regional DTI-ALPS indices were significantly reduced in the hearing impairment group and were inversely correlated with hearing thresholds. In multivariate analysis, both older age and lower DTI-ALPS index remained independently associated with hearing impairment. The combined model incorporating age and DTI-ALPS achieved the best discriminative performance. These findings suggest that hearing impairment is independently associated with reduced glymphatic system function, and that the DTI-ALPS index, particularly when combined with age, may serve as a promising imaging biomarker for age-related hearing decline.

title: QFR-guided versus IVUS-guided with QFR confirmation for drug-coated balloon treatment of non-complex coronary lesions: a single-centre pilot randomised trial
abstract: Abstract Background: Drug-coated balloon (DCB) angioplasty for the treatment of coronary artery lesions relies on adequate lesion pre-treatment, yet the optimal strategy for intraoperative imaging guidance remains unclear. This randomized controlled pilot trial aims to evaluate the feasibility of a strategy combining quantitative flow ratio (QFR) guidance with intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) guidance and QFR validation (IVUS+QFR) in the treatment of non-complex coronary artery lesions with DCB, and to provide estimates of the effect size for follow-up studies. Methods: This study was a prospective, single-center, open-label randomized controlled pilot trial, enrolling a total of 78 patients (82 vessels; 4 patients contributed 2 vessels each). Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to the QFR-guided group (43 vessels) or the IVUS+QFR-guided group (39 vessels). The primary endpoint was immediate post-procedural functional success, defined as a post-PCI QFR ≥ 0.90 assessed offline by the core laboratory. The primary effect measure was the absolute risk difference (RD) and its 95% confidence interval(calculated using a patient-level clustered bootstrap method). Results: All 78 patients completed the assigned protocol, and the primary endpoint data of 82 vessels were fully obtained (100% feasibility). The rate of functional success was 79.1% (34/43) in the QFR-guided group and 84.6% (33/39) in the IVUS+QFR-guided group. The relative difference (RD) between the two groups was −5.5 percentage points (95% CI: −21.3 to 11.7). The odds ratio (OR) adjusted for covariates was 0.58 (95% CI: 0.18–1.85; P = 0.357). The confidence interval is too wide to draw a definitive conclusion regarding the superiority or inferiority of strategy , which is consistent with the exploratory nature of a pilot trial. Conclusions: Both QFR-guided and IVUS+QFR-guided strategies demonstrated complete procedural feasibility in DCB treatment. The effect size estimates and confidence interval precision provided by this study may serve as important references for sample size calculation in future confirmatory trials. Trial registration: Trial registration: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry ChiCTR2400084789 (registered on 24 May 2024; Retrospectively registered).

title: CT-Based Habitat Radiomics and Deep Learning for Predicting Early Response and Survival in Unresectable Hepatocellular Carcinoma Treated with Hepatic Arterial Infusion Chemotherapy plus Lenvatinib and Programmed Death Receptor-1 Inhibitors
abstract: Abstract Background The marked intratumoral heterogeneity of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) leads to substantial variability in treatment response among patients receiving HAIC-FOLFOX combined with lenvatinib and PD-1 inhibitors. This study aimed to develop a multidimensional fusion model integrating habitat radiomics, 2.5D deep learning features, and clinical indicators to predict early objective response and progression-free survival in these patients. Methods This dual-center retrospective study enrolled 240 patients with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma treated with HAIC-FOLFOX combined with lenvatinib and PD-1 inhibitors. Patients from Center 1 were randomly assigned in a 7:3 ratio to a training cohort (n = 112) and an internal validation cohort (n = 49), while 79 patients from Center 2 constituted the independent external testing cohort. Habitat imaging was employed to decompose the tumor into phenotypically distinct subregions via K-means clustering. Radiomics features were then extracted from the whole-tumor region and each habitat subregion on pretreatment contrast-enhanced CT images. Four 2.5D convolutional neural networks were trained for deep feature extraction. Machine learning models, including a combined model constructed through feature-level and decision-level fusion, were evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration curves, and decision curve analysis. SHapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) analysis was performed for model interpretability. Results The combined model achieved AUCs of 0.911 (95% CI: 0.855–0.967), 0.883 (95% CI: 0.780–0.987), and 0.871 (95% CI: 0.792–0.949) in the training, internal validation, and external testing cohorts, respectively. Calibration curves demonstrated favorable agreement between predicted and observed outcomes. Decision curve analysis confirmed higher net clinical benefit for the combined model. DeLong's test showed the combined model significantly outperformed all other models in the external testing cohort (all P < 0.05). The model-derived risk stratification effectively discriminated progression-free survival across all three cohorts (all log-rank P < 0.001). Conclusion The combined model offers a noninvasive tool for pretreatment prediction of both early objective response and progression-free survival in patients with unresectable HCC undergoing HAIC combined with lenvatinib and PD-1 inhibitors, potentially informing individualized treatment decisions.

title: SFCT-Net: A Wavelet-Based Spatial-Frequency Signal Reconstruction Framework for Robust Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Abstract Medical ultrasound and dermoscopic images can be interpreted as corrupted signals in both spatial and frequency domains, presenting profound challenges for automated segmentation due to intrinsic sensor degradations such as acoustic speckle noise and low-frequency contrast attenuation. In conventional automated segmentation, treating this task purely as a spatial-domain pixel classification problem often relying on bilinear interpolation or transposed convolutions for decoding inevitably acts as a suboptimal low-pass filter. This spatial manipulation triggers severe frequency aliasing, severely degrading fragile high-frequency anatomical boundaries during the signal reconstruction process. To address this limitation, we redefine medical image segmentation as a spatial-frequency signal reconstruction problem and propose a robust wavelet-domain framework, SFCT-Net. To effectively capture features without sequential degradation, we deploy synchronized convolutional and self-attention streams, introducing an Asymmetric Cross-Interaction Module (ACIM) to dynamically calibrate and align these heterogeneous semantics. Crucially, as the primary signal reconstruction operator, we introduce the Wavelet-Driven Reconstruction Module (WRM). By seamlessly embedding the 2D Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT), WRM explicitly applies frequency decoupling, orthogonally isolating low-frequency semantic components from high-frequency edge contours. This paradigm executes targeted noise suppression and maintains strong structural consistency entirely within the frequency domain.Extensive evaluations on ten public medical image datasets indicate that the proposed framework consistently achieves competitive segmentation performance with improved boundary preservation and robust generalization across multiple imaging modalities.

title: Biopsies from Normal-Appearing Mucosa in Pediatric Upper GI Endoscopy: What Do They Tell Us?
abstract: Abstract Purpose: Histopathological abnormalities may be detected despite normal endoscopic findings in pediatric upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy. However, the clinical value of routine biopsies from macroscopically normal mucosa remains uncertain. We aimed to evaluate the impact of such biopsies on diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up. Methods: We conducted a retrospective study of children undergoing upper GI endoscopy at a tertiary care center over a one-year period. Biopsies obtained from macroscopically normal esophageal, gastric, and duodenal mucosa were analyzed. Biopsy findings were assessed for their impact on clinical management, defined as any change in treatment or follow-up. Results were evaluated according to both the number of affected patients and the total number of biopsy specimens. Results: A total of 802 endoscopies were included. Biopsies from normal-appearing mucosa were obtained in 577 patients (71.9%), yielding 2,055 biopsy specimens. Histopathological findings altered clinical management in 60 patients (10.4%). At the biopsy level, 116 specimens (5.6%) revealed clinically relevant findings, whereas 542 (26.4%) showed inflammatory changes without clinical impact and 1,397 (68.0%) were histologically normal. Most management-changing findings were related to Helicobacter pylori infection (26/60). Clinical impact varied according to presenting symptoms and biopsy site. Conclusions: Routine biopsy of macroscopically normal mucosa during pediatric upper GI endoscopy rarely influences clinical management. A selective biopsy strategy guided by presenting symptoms, clinical suspicion, and established guideline recommendations may optimize diagnostic yield while reducing unnecessary procedures.

title: Preoperative Prediction of Vascular Invasion in Breast Cancer Based on Habitat-Based Radiomics Integrating Intratumoral and Multidimensional Peritumoral Features: A Multicenter DCE-MRI Study
abstract: Abstract Background: Lymphatic vessel invasion (LVI) is widely recognized as an indicator of breast cancer aggressiveness and metastatic potential; however, the lack of non-invasive tools capable of capturing intratumoral and peritumoral heterogeneity continues to pose challenges for reliable preoperative prediction. Purpose: The aim of this study is to develop and rigorously validate a multimodal fusion model that integrates traditional radiomics, image features derived from habitat-based imaging, and clinical risk factors to enable non-invasive preoperative prediction of lymphatic vessel invasion (LVI) in breast cancer. Method: This retrospective study included 742 patients from two independent centers. Data from Center 1 (n = 628) were randomly split in a 7:3 ratio into a training set (n = 439) and an internal validation set (n = 189); Center 2 (n = 114) served as an independent external validation set. A comprehensive radiomic analysis was performed on DCE-MRI data, covering the intratumoral region and peritumoral expansion at five increasing distances (1, 3, 5, 7, and 10 mm). Tumor functional subregions (habitats) were identified using K-means clustering. The performance of nine machine learning algorithms was compared, and the optimal ExtraTrees habitat features were fused with independent clinical predictors (menopausal status and sentinel lymph node status) to construct the final combined model. Discrimination ability was assessed using AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity, while calibration and clinical utility were evaluated through calibration curve and decision curve analyses. Results: In the comparison of tumor-peripheral distances, the 7-mm combined with AdaBoost model demonstrated relatively good generalization ability (AUC of 0.674 in the external validation set), but the differences among the various distances were not statistically significant. Multivariate analysis revealed that menopausal status and sentinel lymph node status were independent predictors of LVI. The multimodal fusion model achieved the most balanced overall performance, with an AUC of 0.740 (95% CI: 0.646–0.834) in the independent external validation set, a precision of 72.8%, and a sensitivity as high as 71.2%. Although the AUC of the clinical-only model was slightly higher (0.713), the fusion model demonstrated significantly superior sensitivity (71.2% vs. 64.4%). The model showed good calibration, and ROC curve analysis confirmed that it provided clinical net benefit within a threshold probability range of 0.2–0.6. Conclusion: DCE-MRI-based in-tumor and peritumoral microenvironment omics analysis, combined with readily available clinical variables, offers a promising non-invasive approach for preoperative risk stratification of lymphatic vessel invasion (LVI) in breast cancer. This multimodal framework has undergone cross-device external validation and is expected to support personalized treatment decisions for breast cancer.

title: A case report of vulvar teratoma
abstract: Abstract Background Teratomas composed of tissues derived from all three germ layers are germ cell tumors originating from totipotent stem cells. While gonadal teratomas are common, extragonadal teratomas account for approximately 15% of all cases, with vulvar localization being exceptionally rare. To date, only a limited number of vulvar teratoma cases have been reported in the international literature. Case: A 19-year-old female presented with a vulvar mass first noted at birth that had progressively enlarged with age. Over the preceding year, the patient experienced intermittent inflammation and recurrent ulceration secondary to friction, accompanied by mild dysuria. Physical examination revealed a pedunculated mass measuring 5 × 4 cm situated between the clitoris and urethral meatus, together with a 2 × 2 cm urethral caruncle. Multimodal imaging including ultrasonography, computed tomography, and magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a mixed-echogenicity exophytic mass containing mesenteric and bowel-like structures with a prominent vascular pedicle extending toward the urethra and bladder trigone. The preoperative differential diagnosis included external parasitic twin (fetus in fetu) versus vulvar teratoma. The patient underwent complete surgical excision of the vulvar mass and the urethral caruncle under general anesthesia. Histopathological examination confirmed the diagnosis of a mature teratoma. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed CK8/18 (+), CK20 (+), CDX-2 (+), Vimentin (+), and a Ki-67 proliferation index of less than 10%. The postoperative course was uneventful. At one-month follow-up, the wound had healed completely with restoration of normal vulvar anatomy and preserved physiological function. Conclusion Mature teratoma of the vulva is a rare extragonadal neoplasm that may be misdiagnosed on imaging as a parasitic twin owing to overlapping radiological features. Complete surgical excision remains the treatment of choice and is associated with favorable outcomes. originalAbstract: Background Teratomas composed of tissues derived from all three germ layers are germ cell tumors originating from totipotent stem cells. title: Pyogenic Liver Abscess Following ERCP and Biliary Stenting: A Case Series of Two Patients and Clinical Implications
abstract: Abstract Introduction: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is a critical diagnostic and therapeutic modality for choledocholithiasis, acute cholangitis, and obstructive jaundice. Although pyogenic liver abscess is a rare complication following ERCP, it carries significant clinical implications. We present two cases of pyogenic liver abscess developing after ERCP and biliary stent-related procedures in patients with choledocholithiasis. Case Presentation: Case 1 involved a 42-year-old female who developed a liver abscess in segment 4 following laparoscopic cholecystectomy, common bile duct exploration, intraoperative ERCP with stent placement, primary closure of the common bile duct, and drainage of a segment 4 hepatic cyst. The abscess manifested after stent removal and balloon sweeping of the bile duct, presenting with right upper quadrant pain, chills, and fever up to 39°C. Computed tomography (CT) confirmed a liver abscess in segment 4. Case 2 involved a 62-year-old male who underwent ERCP with sphincterotomy, basket stone extraction, and biliary stent placement for choledocholithiasis with obstructive jaundice. On postoperative day 6, he developed right upper quadrant pain, chills, and fever up to 39°C. CT revealed a new 32 mm × 26 mm abscess in the right hepatic lobe, with markedly elevated procalcitonin (63.7 ng/mL) and renal dysfunction. Both patients improved after percutaneous drainage, and Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae were isolated from abscess cultures in both cases. Conclusion: Although rare, pyogenic liver abscess should be considered in patients with biliary infection, stent placement or removal, sphincterotomy, complex biliary surgery, or pre-existing hepatic cystic lesions following ERCP. Early imaging evaluation with ultrasonography or contrast-enhanced CT is warranted when postoperative abdominal pain, chills, high fever, elevated inflammatory markers, or cholestasis abnormalities occur. Image-guided percutaneous drainage, combined with appropriate antimicrobial therapy, serves as an effective minimally invasive intervention for source control.
